# How transcripts get compared, and why novel-isoform counts move

Novel-isoform percentages in the literature range from a few per cent to more
than half of everything detected, sometimes for the same input data. The spread
comes mostly from how two transcripts get compared and what they get compared
against, rather than from a disagreement about biology. This walkthrough works
through the comparison itself so that the numbers in the main chapters are
readable.

You do not need this to follow the argument anywhere in the book. Read it if you
want to know why a claim like "a third of detected transcripts were novel"
is incomplete without its denominator.

## What a transcript model actually is

Strip away the sequence and a transcript model is a short list of coordinates:
the start, the end, and the positions where introns were removed. For a
transcript with four exons on one chromosome:

```
exon    ========        =====      ====        =========
        1000-1200    1500-1600  1900-1980   2400-2700
intron          1200-1500   1600-1900  1980-2400
```

The ordered list of internal intron boundaries, here
`(1200, 1500), (1600, 1900), (1980, 2400)`, is the **intron chain**. It records
which splice junctions occurred, and that they occurred *in the same
molecule*.

That last point is the whole reason long reads changed this field. A short-read
experiment can observe all three of those junctions in a sample and still not
establish that any single molecule used all three. Each junction is observed,
and the combination of them is an inference.

## Comparing two chains

To ask whether two transcripts are the same, walk their intron chains in
parallel and compare coordinates pairwise. The comparison is exact, and a single
base of difference at one splice site makes two chains different.

Take an annotated transcript and an observed one:

```
annotated   (1200,1500)  (1600,1900)  (1980,2400)
observed    (1200,1500)  (1600,1900)  (1980,2400)      -> same chain
observed    (1200,1500)  (1600,1900)  (1980,2401)      -> different chain
observed    (1200,1500)  (1600,1900)                   -> contained in the chain
observed    (1200,1500)  (1700,1900)  (1980,2400)      -> different chain
```

The second row is the one that moves novelty counts. One base at one acceptor
site makes the transcript formally novel. Whether that base is biology or an
alignment artifact is a separate question, and often an unanswerable one for a
single read.

The third row is different in kind. Nothing contradicts the annotation; the
observation is just shorter. A read that stops early because the molecule
fragmented produces exactly this, and so does a genuinely shorter transcript.
The comparison cannot tell them apart, which is why the categories below exist.

## The categories, and what each one is sensitive to

Transcript comparison tools sort observations into classes. The names vary, but
the distinctions are consistent:

**Full splice match.** Every internal junction matches an annotated transcript
exactly. Sensitive to single-base alignment error at splice sites, and to which
annotation release you used.

**Incomplete splice match.** The observed chain is a contiguous subset of an
annotated chain, as in row three above. Inflated by anything that truncates
molecules or reads: RNA degradation, incomplete reverse transcription, internal
priming on an A-rich stretch, or reads that fail to span the full transcript.

**Novel in catalog.** All junctions individually exist in the annotation, but this
particular combination does not. This class is where short-read ambiguity used to
live, and it is the class where real combinatorial novelty would show up. It is
also the class most affected by the denominator question below.

**Novel not in catalog.** At least one junction is itself unannotated. Most
sensitive to alignment quality, and the class where a single mismapped read can
manufacture a novel isoform.

A pipeline that aligns slightly differently will move transcripts between
classes without any change in the data. Truncation artifacts and real short
isoforms also land in the same bin, so the incomplete-splice-match count is
never a clean biological quantity.

## The denominator

Most of the spread in published numbers comes from the reference. "Novel" means
"not in whatever it was compared against", and that reference varies.

The same observed transcripts can be compared against:

- a single annotation release, and novelty reflects what that release happened to contain
- a different release of the same annotation, and the number changes, because releases differ
- a different annotation project entirely, and it changes again, because projects use different inclusion rules
- a large population of other long-read transcriptomes, and it collapses

That last case is the sharpest demonstration. Re-scoring one benchmark sample
against a catalog built from roughly a thousand long-read datasets instead of
against a reference annotation cut the apparent novel fraction from somewhere in
the 27 to 52 per cent range down to 2 to 5 per cent [@zheng2026isopedia]. The
transcripts are the same in both scorings, and only the question changed, from
asking whether this is in the annotation to asking whether anyone else has ever
seen it.

A transcript absent from an annotation but present in hundreds of independent
samples is unannotated rather than novel, which is a statement about the
annotation.

## What to take back to the chapters

When you read a novel-isoform percentage anywhere, three things determine it
before biology gets a say: which annotation was the denominator, what
read-support threshold was applied, and how the aligner placed splice sites. A
number without those is not comparable to another number.

This is also why pipeline-to-pipeline agreement is low in benchmarking studies
while PCR validation rates stay high. Pipelines disagree about which novel
isoforms to report, and the ones they report are frequently real.
